3. Synchro plates test: Perform a countermovement jump at 90° of knee flexion. During the landing phase, stop
                         the movement at 90° of knee flexion.
                       4. Modified triple leg jumping test: Perform 3 jumps in the frontal plane with the injured leg and then with the
                         noninjured leg.
                       5. Modified side-step cutting test: After a run of 5 m, touch a skittle, and make a change in direction at 90°.
                         Then run at maximum speed to a second skittle 5 m away.
                       6. Sprint braking test: Sprint at maximum speed for 30 m. Then sprint 30 m at 90% of maximum speed to
                         a skittle. Repeat a second trial with a skittle at 6 m and then 4 m.
                       7. Illinois agility test: Follow a specific path at maximum speed.
                       8. Modified Illinois agility test: Follow a specific path at maximum speed with a ball.
Bortone9 (2021)        Standardized postoperative and rehabilitation protocol
Chaves12 (2012)        Functional rehabilitation with an accelerated protocol
Della Villa13 (2012)   Initial phases of rehabilitation: Patients began engaging in gymnasium and pool exercises that targeted pain,
                         swelling, range of motion, proprioception, strength, and aerobic fitness. Early soccer-specific exercises were
                         performed.
                       Final phases of rehabilitation: Patients attended 90-min OFR sessions 2 to 5 d/wk. The protocol consisted of 5
                         phases of progressive soccer-specific exercises including strength training, conditioning, and increased
                         musculoskeletal and neuromechanical functional demands.
Herrington21 (2018)    Rehabilitation on a full-time basis within their professional soccer club
Jacopetti23 (2016)     Same rehabilitation protocol for all patients
Lee29 (2016)           The accelerated rehabilitation program suggested by Shelbourne and Nitz46 was modified and applied in 2-h
                         sessions 5 times a week. Phase 1 was intended to relieve inflammation and edema. Phase 2 aimed to increase
                         range of motion. Phase 3 focused on increasing muscle strength. Phase 4 sought to improve balance ability.
Mohammadi32 (2013)     Accelerated rehabilitation protocol that focused on strengthening, balance, proprioception, stability, agility,
                         plyometrics, and RTP training
Nambi36 (2021)         Rehabilitation protocol that focused on strengthening the quadriceps and hamstring muscles, with specific
                         criteria for progression
Olivier37 (2010)       At 1-2 wk: The priority was to decrease pain and swelling and to restore full knee extension and quadriceps
                         strength.
                       At 2-6 wk: The plan was to continue increasing knee range of motion and weightbearing and gaining hamstring
                         and quadriceps control. Additionally, gait and static proprioception exercises were initiated.
                       OLC: In addition to the above exercises, the untreated leg was engaged in an OLC training program. The OLC
                         training program consisted of 3 sessions a week for 6 wk.
Ozdemir38 (2018)       During the rehabilitation program, patients had sessions 4 to 6 times a week. Angular velocity with exercises
                         was decreased throughout training. The angular velocity was 240 deg/s at 1 wk, 180 to 150 deg/s at 2 wk, 120
                         deg/s at 3 and 4 wk, and 60 deg/s at 5 and 6 wk.
Rahova40 (2022)        The 6-mo rehabilitation program consisted of strengthening, stretching, isometric, isotonic, balance and
                         coordination, proprioception, and plyometric exercises. Running and cycling were also initiated.
Read41 (2020)          Standardized rehabilitation protocol
Read42 (2020)          Rehabilitation protocol with previous 6-m hop exercises
Read43 (2022)          Criteria-based rehabilitation program designed by van Grinsven et al52 combined with a sports-specific phase
                         of reconditioning
Rudroff45 (2003)       The rehabilitation protocol lasted 6 wk. The initial program consisted of daily passive and active treatments.
                         After the patients achieved full range of motion, weight training and an accelerated rehabilitation program
                         that focused on muscle coordination were started.
Thomson51 (2018)       Criteria-based rehabilitation program
van Melick54 (2019)    Rehabilitation sessions 2 to 3 times a week based on ACLR practice guidelines that emphasized functional
                         goal–based criteria

Welling57 (2019)            The strength training protocol was based on American College of Sports Medicine principles and rehabilitation
                             guidelines that emphasized individualized exercises. The initial phase focused on attaining full knee
                             extension and pain reduction and performing quadriceps activation exercises. The second phase at 10 to 14
                             wk was composed of muscular endurance exercises. The third phase at 12 to 14 wk aimed to improve strength
                             and normalize leg strength symmetry. Endurance training was continued with the addition of balance
                             exercises, running, and jump-landing techniques. The fourth phase at 14 to 16 wk aimed to improve knee
                             extension and flexion muscle strength deficits. The same exercises and variations were repeated from the
                             previous stages. This phase finished with OFR and RTP.

                             pain and swelling and improve range of motion, proprioception, strength, and aerobic fitness. Early soccer-
                             specific exercises were also used. The final phases comprised OFR. Each OFR session lasted 90 min, 2 to 5 d/
                             wk, and was composed of 5 stages. Exercises included strength training, conditioning, and increased
                             functional demands of musculoskeletal and neuromechanical components involved in recovery after ACLR.

   "doi":"10.1177/03635465241233161",
   "abstract":"This systematic review of 23 studies (874 soccer players after ACL reconstruction) looked for rehabilitation protocols and functional tests that support return to play in soccer. The authors found no consensus, with wide heterogeneity in protocols and test batteries, return-to-play times of 3 to 8 months, and few reports of complications or long-term follow-up.",
   "tldr":"Rehabilitation and return-to-play testing after ACL reconstruction in soccer lack standardization, and the evidence is small, mostly retrospective and male-dominated. Staff should document and justify their own test batteries and progression criteria rather than adopt a protocol from this review.",
   "methods":"Systematic review of PubMed, Embase and CENTRAL following PRISMA, with two independent reviewers for selection and data extraction. Original studies at level of evidence 1 to 4 that reported rehabilitation protocols, knee rehabilitation metrics or clinical outcomes in soccer players after ACL reconstruction were included. Non-randomized studies were appraised with MINORS and the two RCTs with RoB 2. Weighted means and pooled percentages were calculated for participant characteristics.",
   "findings":"Twenty-three studies (874 players) were included, with 5 accelerated and 7 criterion-based protocols and 11 unclassified. Two studies used all three test batteries (strength, hop and movement quality), eight used two, twelve used one and one used none. Mean surgery-to-return-to-play times ranged from 3 to 8 months. Only one study reported a return rate (95% returned to the same professional level), two reported complications, and all nine studies reporting PROMs showed significant improvement.",
   "limitations":"Heterogeneity in sample size, protocols and outcomes limited pooling, and there was little long-term follow-up (one study at four years). Most studies were retrospective, female players were under-represented, and the authors note the findings may not apply to other sports. The review only included soccer studies and did not assess the predictive value of any test.",
   "practicalImplications":"Clinicians can see that strength, hop and movement-quality batteries are common, but no single battery or criteria set has been shown to predict safe return. Programs should set and record their own progression criteria, and test results should be interpreted alongside clinical examination and the athlete's history.",
   "athleteDev":"Performance Application: the review supports using multi-domain test batteries during rehabilitation, but it does not give validated thresholds or identify which tests predict on-field performance, so any cut-off has to come from the program itself.",
   "rtp":"Return to Sport Application: the study reports mean surgery-to-return-to-play times of 3 to 8 months, but it reports return rates in only one study and complications in two, so it cannot be used to set a clearance date, a return-rate target or the claim that a specific test makes return safe."

Rehabilitation and Return to Sport in Athletes


                Rehabilitation and Return to Sport Testing After
               Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction: Where
                                Are We in 2022?
          Alli Gokeler, Ph.D., P.T., Bart Dingenen, Ph.D., P.T., and Timothy E. Hewett, Ph.D.




Abstract: Athletes who sustain an anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury often opt for an ACL reconstruction (ACLR)
with the goal and expectation to return to sports at the preinjury level. The proportion of athletes who successfully return
to preinjury-level sport is low and disappointing, whereas the rate of second ACL injury in athletes under the age of 20 has
been reported to be as high as 40% after return to sport (RTS). Although in recent years, new insights pertaining to RTS
have been published, the lack of validity of RTS criteria after ACLR remain. The purpose of this clinical commentary is to
present a critical overview of the current literature on RTS testing after ACLR.

 "evidenceSummary":"A clinical commentary that gives a critical overview of the literature on return-to-sport (RTS) testing after ACL reconstruction, covering strength (limb symmetry index), hop tests, movement quality, psychological readiness, rehabilitation content, timing and the consequences of test results. It cites a proportional meta-analysis in which 23% of patients passed RTS test batteries before return to sport, and it reports that passing criteria reduced graft rupture risk by 60% but raised contralateral rupture risk by 235%, as the cited review found.",
 "screeningLimitations":"The paper is labelled a clinical commentary and describes no literature search, so it is coded as a narrative review of cited studies, not a structured evidence synthesis. Its arguments rely on cited figures, some from one meta-analysis and one cohort, and the abstract's claim of up to 40% second ACL injury in athletes under 20 differs from the body, which attributes 40% to men's Australian football.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could read the commentary's critique as proof that current RTS test batteries are invalid and should be abandoned, when the authors themselves call for better validated criteria and only summarize existing evidence.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2022,
   "citation":"Gokeler A, Dingenen B, Hewett TE. Rehabilitation and Return to Sport Testing After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction: Where Are We in 2022? Arthroscopy, Sports Medicine, and Rehabilitation. 2022;4(1):e77-e82.",
   "doi":"10.1016/j.asmr.2021.10.025",
   "abstract":"Athletes after ACL reconstruction often aim to return to preinjury sport, but few do, and second ACL injury rates are high after return. This clinical commentary reviews the current literature on RTS testing after ACL reconstruction and concludes that the validity of RTS criteria remains uncertain.",
   "tldr":"Current return-to-sport test batteries after ACL reconstruction have uncertain validity, and common cut-offs such as a 90% limb symmetry index do not capture knee function. Staff should treat a passed test battery as one input to a clinical decision, not as clearance on its own.",
   "methods":"Clinical commentary giving a critical overview of the literature on RTS testing after ACL reconstruction. The paper describes no systematic search, and its evidence is drawn from the cited studies and meta-analyses. Sections cover strength, hop tests, movement quality, psychological factors, rehabilitation approach, timing and consequences of testing.",
   "findings":"The authors cite a meta-analysis in which only 23% of patients passed RTS test batteries before return, and report that passing criteria reduced subsequent graft rupture risk by 60% but raised contralateral rupture risk by 235%. Only 14% of patients reached an LSI of 100% for strength at two years, and 60% of patients showed abnormal landing kinematics even though 72.3% passed an LSI above 90% on hop tests. A test battery with an 80% pass rate per test falls to 64% for two tests and 51% for three.",
   "limitations":"The commentary offers a critical narrative rather than a formal evidence grade, and its key claims depend on the cited studies. The abstract's 40% second ACL injury rate for athletes under 20 differs from the body, which attributes the 40% figure to men's Australian football. Exposure to high-risk activity after testing is often unreported, so test validity cannot be judged fully from these studies.",
   "practicalImplications":"Use a multi-domain battery (strength, hop and movement quality) but do not rely on a single limb symmetry cut-off, because a passed LSI can coexist with abnormal landing mechanics. Record the athlete's exposure after clearance, since the authors argue that second-injury risk depends on what athletes do after testing.",
   "athleteDev":"Performance Application: the commentary supports measuring absolute strength and movement quality as well as limb symmetry during rehabilitation, because symmetry can mask deficits in both limbs. It does not provide validated performance thresholds.",
   "rtp":"Return to Sport Application: the paper shows that current RTS batteries have uncertain validity and that passing them does not reliably identify athletes at risk of second ACL injury. It cannot be used to set a specific LSI threshold, a clearance date or a required test pass rate as a standalone decision rule."
 }
}

19	Background The age of first exposure (AFE) to American football participation is a growing concern for late-life function.
20	Mixed evidence exists surrounding AFE and may be attributed to varied methods employed across studies.
21	Objective To examine the associations between AFE to American football participation with measures of cognitive, behav-
22	ioral, and physical function and brain-related medical diagnoses across age categories among former National Football
23	League players.
24	Methods We conducted a cross-sectional survey of 1784 former players (age: 52.3 ± 16.3 years, AFE: 11.3 ± 2.9 years, years
25	of football: 17.5 ± 4.5 years, 86.9% ≥ one lifetime concussion). Players completed a general health questionnaire recording
26	demographics, football playing history (including AFE), and diagnoses (anxiety, depression, any form of dementia, mild
27	cognitive impairment). Players completed Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System (PROMIS) meas-
28	ures assessing domains of cognitive and physical function, anxiety, depression, sleep disturbance, pain interference, and
29	emotional-behavioral dyscontrol. Multivariable linear and binomial regression models were used to examine the associations
30	of AFE and age with PROMIS outcomes and diagnoses, respectively.
31	Results No significant AFE by age interactions were detected for PROMIS outcomes (p ≥ 0.066) or diagnoses (p ≥ 0.147).

Relating American Football Age of First Exposure to Patient‑Reported
Outcomes and Medical Diagnoses Among Former National Football
League Players: An NFL‑LONG study
Landon B. Lempke1,2,3 · Samuel R. Walton4 · Benjamin L. Brett5 · Avinash Chandran6 · J. D. DeFreese4 ·
Rebekah Mannix7,8 · Ruben J. Echemendia9,10 · Michael A. McCrea5 · Kevin M. Guskiewicz4 · William P. Meehan III1,2 ·
Zachary Yukio Kerr4

Accepted: 3 November 2022

Abstract
Background The age of first exposure (AFE) to American football participation is a growing concern for late-life function.
Mixed evidence exists surrounding AFE and may be attributed to varied methods employed across studies.
Objective To examine the associations between AFE to American football participation with measures of cognitive, behav-
ioral, and physical function and brain-related medical diagnoses across age categories among former National Football
League players.
Methods We conducted a cross-sectional survey of 1784 former players (age: 52.3 ± 16.3 years, AFE: 11.3 ± 2.9 years, years
of football: 17.5 ± 4.5 years, 86.9% ≥ one lifetime concussion). Players completed a general health questionnaire recording
demographics, football playing history (including AFE), and diagnoses (anxiety, depression, any form of dementia, mild
cognitive impairment). Players completed Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System (PROMIS) meas-
ures assessing domains of cognitive and physical function, anxiety, depression, sleep disturbance, pain interference, and
emotional-behavioral dyscontrol. Multivariable linear and binomial regression models were used to examine the associations
of AFE and age with PROMIS outcomes and diagnoses, respectively.
Results No significant AFE by age interactions were detected for PROMIS outcomes (p ≥ 0.066) or diagnoses (p ≥ 0.147).
Younger AFE associated with higher PROMIS scores of anxiety (B = − 0.22, p = 0.016), depression (B = − 0.22, p = 0.010),
sleep disturbances (B = − 0.16, p = 0.007), pain interference (B = − 0.19, p = 0.014), and emotional-behavioral dyscontrol
(B = − 0.22, p = 0.019). Age was associated with all PROMIS outcomes (p ≤ 0.042). AFE was not associated with the preva-
lence of anxiety, depression, dementia, or mild cognitive impairment (p ≥ 0.449), while age was (p ≤ 0.013).
Conclusions AFE was significantly associated with PROMIS outcomes, albeit low-strength associations (i.e., effect sizes),
but not with diagnoses. Our findings indicate AFE is a significant but minor contributing factor for health-related quality
of life in this cohort. Future work should incorporate additional characterizations of cumulative head impacts and related
factors when examining long-term outcomes associated with football participation.

      Relationship Between Preseason Training Load and In-Season
              Availability in Elite Australian Football Players
                                       Nick B. Murray, Tim J. Gabbett, and Andrew D. Townshend

     Objectives: To investigate the relationship between the proportion of preseason training sessions completed and load and injury
     during the ensuing Australian Football League season. Design: Single-cohort, observational study. Methods: Forty-six elite male
     Australian football players from 1 club participated. Players were divided into 3 equal groups based on the amount of preseason
     training completed (high [HTL], >85% sessions completed; medium [MTL], 50–85% sessions completed; and low [LTL], <50%
     sessions completed). Global positioning system (GPS) technology was used to record training and game loads, with all injuries
     recorded and classified by club medical staff. Differences between groups were analyzed using a 2-way (group × training/com-
     petition phase) repeated-measures ANOVA, along with magnitude-based inferences. Injury incidence was expressed as injuries
     per 1000 h. Results: The HTL and MTL groups completed a greater proportion of in-season training sessions (81.1% and 74.2%)
     and matches (76.7% and 76.1%) than the LTL (56.9% and 52.7%) group. Total distance and player load were significantly greater
     during the first half of the in-season period for the HTL (P = .03, ES = 0.88) and MTL (P = .02, ES = 0.93) groups than the LTL
     group. The relative risk of injury for the LTL group (26.8/1000 h) was 1.9 times greater than that for the HTL group (14.2/1000
     h) (χ2 = 3.48, df = 2, P = .17). Conclusions: Completing a greater proportion of preseason training resulted in higher training
     loads and greater participation in training and competition during the competitive phase of the season.

     Keywords: GPS, competition, injury

 "decision":"INCLUDE",

 "doiMissing":false,
 "identityCheck":"Title in text 'Relationship Between Preseason Training Load and In-Season Availability in Elite Australian Football Players' matches the filename; International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance 2017 original investigation.",
 "confidence":"high",
 "studyDesign":"Cohort Study",
 "primaryDomain":"Training & Performance",
 "domains":["Training & Performance","Monitoring & Technology","Sports Medicine & Injury"],
 "audiences":["Performance","Athletic Training","Sports Medicine","Research & Analytics"],
 "sports":["Other Sport"],
 "populations":["Professional / Elite","Male Athletes"],
 "evidenceSummary":"A single-cohort observational study of 46 elite male Australian Football League players from one club, divided into thirds by the share of preseason sessions completed (high >85%, n=15; medium 50 to 84.9%, n=16; low <50%, n=15). GPS-derived in-season loads, match availability and injuries were compared. The authors report that the high and medium groups covered more total distance and player load in the first half of the season than the low group (P=.02 to .03), and were available for 76.7% and 76.1% of matches versus 52.7% for the low group, while injury rates of 14.2, 17.7 and 26.8 per 1000 h did not differ significantly (chi-square P=.17).",
 "screeningLimitations":"The study covers one club and one season with only 50 in-season injuries, so the injury comparison is underpowered. Groups were formed by preseason completion, which is linked to rehabilitation time (46% of preseason in the low group versus 4.6% in the high group), so injury or rehabilitation status may explain the differences. No internal load measures were included.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could read the lower injury rate in the high-completion group as proof that completing preseason training prevents injuries, when the injury difference was not significant and the groups differed in rehabilitation time before the season.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2017,
   "citation":"Murray NB, Gabbett TJ, Townshend AD. Relationship Between Preseason Training Load and In-Season Availability in Elite Australian Football Players. Int J Sports Physiol Perform. 2017;12(6):749-755.",
   "doi":"10.1123/ijspp.2015-0806",
   "abstract":"In 46 elite male AFL players from one club, the share of preseason sessions completed was linked to higher GPS training loads, more in-season training and match availability, and lower injury rates that were not statistically significant. Players who completed less than half of preseason training had the highest injury rate (26.8 per 1000 h versus 14.2 in the high-completion group).",
   "tldr":"Elite AFL players who completed more of their preseason training carried higher training loads into the season and were available for more matches. Staff should prioritize preseason completion, while recognizing that the injury difference between groups was not statistically significant.",
   "methods":"Single-cohort observational study of 46 male AFL players. Players were grouped by the percentage of main preseason sessions completed (high >85%, medium 50 to 84.9%, low <50%). A 10-Hz GPS unit with accelerometer recorded total, low, moderate, high and very-high-speed distance and player load in training and matches. Injuries that caused a missed match were logged by club medical staff and expressed per 1000 h. Group and phase effects were analysed with two-way repeated-measures ANOVA, magnitude-based inferences and chi-square tests.",
   "findings":"Preseason training loads were about 1.3 times higher than in-season (P=.02). In the first half of the season, high and medium groups covered significantly more total distance (P=.03 and P=.02) and had higher player load (P=.03 and P=.02) than the low group. Match availability was 76.7% (high), 76.1% (medium) and 52.7% (low). Injury rates were 14.2, 17.7 and 26.8 per 1000 h, a difference that was not significant (chi-square=3.48, P=.17), across 50 in-season injuries.",
   "limitations":"Data come from one club and one season with 50 injuries, which limits power and generalizability. Groups were not randomized, and low-completion players spent far more of the preseason in rehabilitation, so causation cannot be inferred. Internal load was not measured, and the paper calls the 1.9-fold injury ratio a relative risk when it is a ratio of rates.",
   "practicalApplications":"",
   "practicalImplications":"Strength and conditioning staff can use preseason completion as a monitoring signal, since players who completed less preseason training had lower in-season loads and fewer match appearances. Strategies that keep players in the main program during preseason, rather than in rehabilitation or modified sessions, are the practical target.",
   "athleteDev":"Performance Application: players who complete more of the planned preseason program carry higher GPS distance and player load into the season and miss fewer matches, so preseason participation should be treated as a performance priority.",
   "rtp":"Return to Sport Application: the study does not measure return-to-play criteria or rehabilitation outcomes. Because the low-completion group had far more rehabilitation time, it cannot be used to set return-to-play timelines."
 }
}

46	Published: 26 November 2024               1. Introduction
47	                                                Chronic pain affects approximately 18% of the population in Spain, with an estimated
48	                                          economic cost of 16,000 million euros, representing 25% of GDP (Gross Domestic Prod-
49	                                          uct). Chronic pain is defined as a stressful experience associated with existing or potential
50	Copyright: © 2024 by the authors.
51	                                          tissue damage, with sensory, cognitive, emotional, and social components [1]. This com-
52	Licensee MDPI, Basel, Switzerland.
53	                                          plexity makes the experience of pain a multifaceted phenomenon involving biochemical,
54	This article is an open access article
55	                                          neurological, and subjective factors, which increase susceptibility to the chronification
56	distributed under the terms and
57	conditions of the Creative Commons
58	                                          of pain.
59	Attribution (CC BY) license (https://
60	                                                Among the various types of chronic pain, chronic musculoskeletal pain (CMP) is one of
61	creativecommons.org/licenses/by/
62	                                          the most prevalent, significantly impacting individuals’ physical function and quality of life.
63	4.0/).                                    CMP is characterized by pain originating in muscles, bones, joints, and connective tissues
64	
65	
66	
67	
68	Nutrients 2024, 16, 4061. https://doi.org/10.3390/nu16234061                                                   https://www.mdpi.com/journal/nutrients
69	 Nutrients 2024, 16, 4061                                                                                        2 of 12
70	
71	
72	
73	                           and is frequently associated with conditions such as osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis,
74	                           and fibromyalgia. In addition to biomechanical and inflammatory factors, nutritional
75	                           deficiencies, particularly of vitamin D, have emerged as contributing factors to CMP [2,3].
76	                                Research into CMP has aimed to elucidate the mechanisms underlying pain chronifi-
77	                           cation, including peripheral and central nociceptive sensitization, which involve prolonged
78	                           activation and hypersensitivity of pain pathways [4–6]. Cognitive and emotional factors,
79	                           such as catastrophic thinking and emotional dysregulation, also play critical roles in this
80	                           process [7–9].
81	                                Vitamin D has garnered significant attention for its potential role in managing CMP.
82	                           This secosteroid hormone is involved in calcium homeostasis and skeletal health, but it
83	                           also modulates the immune system and inflammatory pathways. Vitamin D interacts
84	                           with its receptor (VDR) in various immune and muscle cells, promoting the production of
85	                           anti-inflammatory cytokines like IL-10, while reducing pro-inflammatory mediators such
86	                           as TNFα and IL-1 [10]. In the context of CMP, vitamin D deficiency has been linked to
87	                           increased pain perception, impaired muscle strength, and reduced muscle regeneration
88	                           due to oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction [11].
89	                                The recommended doses of vitamin D for musculoskeletal health vary depending
90	                           on age, baseline serum levels, and geographic location. For individuals with deficiency
91	                           (<20 ng/mL serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D), daily doses between 2000 and 4000 IU are
92	                           generally suggested, while maintenance doses of 800–1200 IU per day are recommended
93	                           for prevention in at-risk populations [12,13]. These doses are believed to be effective in
94	                           improving muscle strength, reducing pain, and enhancing overall skeletal health, although
95	                           optimal dosing for chronic musculoskeletal pain specifically requires further study.
96	                                In Spain, low vitamin D concentrations are highly prevalent, exceeding 80% in individ-
97	                           uals over 65 years and 40% in younger populations. This widespread deficiency, combined
98	                           with the mechanistic evidence linking vitamin D to pain modulation, highlights the need
99	                           for further investigation into the relationship between vitamin D levels and CMP [14,15].
100	                                Previous studies have investigated this relationship with conflicting results. For
101	                           example, one study in men aged 40–79 years found lower vitamin D levels in those with
102	                           musculoskeletal pain [16]. However, systematic reviews have been inconclusive due to the
103	                           heterogeneity of results.
104	                                The objective of this study is to investigate the relationship between serum vitamin
105	                           D levels and CMP in adults. The study focuses on examining whether there is a direct
106	                           correlation between low levels of vitamin D and the presence and intensity of CMP, using
107	                           a systematic review of previous studies covering this topic. Additionally, it seeks to
108	                           determine if vitamin D supplementation could play a therapeutic role in managing pain in
109	                           these patients.
110	
111	                           2. Materials and Methods
112	                                The systematic review was conducted following the PRISMA guidelines [17] and
113	                           organized using the PICO framework. Searches were conducted in PubMed, Cochrane,
114	                           and PEDro databases using the following keywords: “Musculoskeletal chronic pain”,
115	                           “fibromyalgia”, “chronic widespread pain”, “vitamin D”, “vitamin D deficiency”, and
116	                           “vitamin D levels”. Observational studies published between 1 January 1990 and 31
117	                           October 2022 were included.
118	
119	                           2.1. Inclusion and Exclusion Criteria
120	                                Studies were included if they involved adults aged 18 years and older suffering from
121	                           chronic musculoskeletal pain, with vitamin D levels assessed via blood tests. Exclusion
122	                           criteria were studies involving participants under 18 years of age and studies evaluating
123	                           pain other than chronic musculoskeletal pain.
124	 Nutrients 2024, 16, 4061                                                                                           3 of 12
125	
126	
127	
128	                           2.2. Primary Outcomes
129	                           •    Pain Intensity: Pain levels were quantified using validated tools such as the Visual Ana-
130	                                logue Scale (VAS) and the Fibromyalgia Impact Questionnaire (FIQ). Specific thresholds
131	                                for categorizing pain intensity (e.g., mild, moderate, severe) were established.
132	                           •    Vitamin D Levels: Serum vitamin D concentrations were measured in ng/mL. Defini-
133	                                tions for vitamin D deficiency (<20 ng/mL), insufficiency (20–30 ng/mL), and sufficiency
134	                                (>30 ng/mL) were standardized according to the Endocrine Society guidelines.
135	
136	                           2.3. Secondary Outcomes
137	                           •    Quality of Life: Assessed using instruments such as the Short Form Health Survey
138	                                (SF-36) and the EuroQol-5D (EQ-5D).
139	                           •    Functional Ability: Measured using the Health Assessment Questionnaire (HAQ) and
140	                                the Oswestry Disability Index (ODI).
141	                           •    Biochemical Markers: Levels of parathyroid hormone (PTH), calcium, and phosphate
142	                                were recorded to provide context on the metabolic impact of vitamin D deficiency.
143	                           •    Sun Exposure and Dietary Intake: Evaluated using validated questionnaires and
144	                                dietary intake records to assess other sources of vitamin D.
145	                           •    Demographic and Baseline Characteristics: Data on age, gender, BMI, baseline pain
146	                                levels, and comorbid conditions were collected to adjust for confounding variables.
147	
148	                           2.4. Quality Assessment
149	                                The quality of the included studies was evaluated using the NIH Quality Assessment
150	                           Tool for Observational Cohort and Cross-Sectional Studies. This tool consists of 14 criteria,
151	                           with each item rated as “cannot determine”, “not applicable”, or “not reported”. Based on
152	                           the overall scoring, studies were classified as “good” (11–14 points), “fair” (5–10 points),
153	                           or “poor” (0–4 points). For case series, the NIH Quality Assessment Tool for Case Series
154	                           Studies was applied.
155	
156	                           2.5. Data Analysis
157	                                The data analysis involved grouping studies according to the presence or absence
158	                           of a control group, the use of sun exposure questionnaires, and the assessment of pain
159	                           levels in relation to vitamin D status. A qualitative analysis was conducted to explore
160	                           the relationships between vitamin D levels and chronic musculoskeletal pain, as well as
161	                           between vitamin D levels and pain intensity.
162	
163	                           3. Results
164	                           3.1. Study Selection
165	                                A total of 30 observational studies investigating the relationship between vitamin D
166	                           levels and chronic musculoskeletal pain in adults were reviewed following the PRISMA
167	                           guideline. These studies were obtained by searching PubMed, Cochrane, and PEDro
168	                           databases, covering the period from 1990 to 2022. The selected studies met the quality
169	                           standards of the NHLBI guidelines.
170	
171	                           3.2. Analysis and Synthesis of Results
172	                                The review focused on qualitatively examining the association between vitamin D
173	                           levels and chronic musculoskeletal pain, differences between men and women, and the
174	                           inverse relationship between vitamin D levels and pain intensity. It differentiated studies
175	                           with control groups from those without, highlighting that those with control groups provide
176	                           more reliable information. The review also considered the timing of blood sample collection
177	                           due to seasonal variations in UVA radiation affecting vitamin D levels, reflecting this in the
178	                           methodological quality of the studies, as shown in Table 1 [18].

                                          uct). Chronic pain is defined as a stressful experience associated with existing or potential

                                                Among the various types of chronic pain, chronic musculoskeletal pain (CMP) is one of
creativecommons.org/licenses/by/

4.0/).                                    CMP is characterized by pain originating in muscles, bones, joints, and connective tissues




Nutrients 2024, 16, 4061. https://doi.org/10.3390/nu16234061                                                   https://www.mdpi.com/journal/nutrients
 Nutrients 2024, 16, 4061                                                                                        2 of 12



                           and is frequently associated with conditions such as osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis,
                           and fibromyalgia. In addition to biomechanical and inflammatory factors, nutritional
                           deficiencies, particularly of vitamin D, have emerged as contributing factors to CMP [2,3].
                                Research into CMP has aimed to elucidate the mechanisms underlying pain chronifi-
                           cation, including peripheral and central nociceptive sensitization, which involve prolonged
                           activation and hypersensitivity of pain pathways [4–6]. Cognitive and emotional factors,
                           such as catastrophic thinking and emotional dysregulation, also play critical roles in this
                           process [7–9].
                                Vitamin D has garnered significant attention for its potential role in managing CMP.
                           This secosteroid hormone is involved in calcium homeostasis and skeletal health, but it
                           also modulates the immune system and inflammatory pathways. Vitamin D interacts
                           with its receptor (VDR) in various immune and muscle cells, promoting the production of
                           anti-inflammatory cytokines like IL-10, while reducing pro-inflammatory mediators such
                           as TNFα and IL-1 [10]. In the context of CMP, vitamin D deficiency has been linked to
                           increased pain perception, impaired muscle strength, and reduced muscle regeneration
                           due to oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction [11].
                                The recommended doses of vitamin D for musculoskeletal health vary depending
                           on age, baseline serum levels, and geographic location. For individuals with deficiency
                           (<20 ng/mL serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D), daily doses between 2000 and 4000 IU are
                           generally suggested, while maintenance doses of 800–1200 IU per day are recommended
                           for prevention in at-risk populations [12,13]. These doses are believed to be effective in
                           improving muscle strength, reducing pain, and enhancing overall skeletal health, although
                           optimal dosing for chronic musculoskeletal pain specifically requires further study.
                                In Spain, low vitamin D concentrations are highly prevalent, exceeding 80% in individ-
                           uals over 65 years and 40% in younger populations. This widespread deficiency, combined
                           with the mechanistic evidence linking vitamin D to pain modulation, highlights the need
                           for further investigation into the relationship between vitamin D levels and CMP [14,15].
                                Previous studies have investigated this relationship with conflicting results. For
                           example, one study in men aged 40–79 years found lower vitamin D levels in those with
                           musculoskeletal pain [16]. However, systematic reviews have been inconclusive due to the
                           heterogeneity of results.
                                The objective of this study is to investigate the relationship between serum vitamin
                           D levels and CMP in adults. The study focuses on examining whether there is a direct
                           correlation between low levels of vitamin D and the presence and intensity of CMP, using
                           a systematic review of previous studies covering this topic. Additionally, it seeks to
                           determine if vitamin D supplementation could play a therapeutic role in managing pain in
                           these patients.

                           2. Materials and Methods
                                The systematic review was conducted following the PRISMA guidelines [17] and
                           organized using the PICO framework. Searches were conducted in PubMed, Cochrane,
                           and PEDro databases using the following keywords: “Musculoskeletal chronic pain”,
                           “fibromyalgia”, “chronic widespread pain”, “vitamin D”, “vitamin D deficiency”, and
                           “vitamin D levels”. Observational studies published between 1 January 1990 and 31
                           October 2022 were included.

                           2.1. Inclusion and Exclusion Criteria
                                Studies were included if they involved adults aged 18 years and older suffering from
                           chronic musculoskeletal pain, with vitamin D levels assessed via blood tests. Exclusion
                           criteria were studies involving participants under 18 years of age and studies evaluating
                           pain other than chronic musculoskeletal pain.
 Nutrients 2024, 16, 4061                                                                                           3 of 12



                           2.2. Primary Outcomes
                           •    Pain Intensity: Pain levels were quantified using validated tools such as the Visual Ana-
                                logue Scale (VAS) and the Fibromyalgia Impact Questionnaire (FIQ). Specific thresholds
                                for categorizing pain intensity (e.g., mild, moderate, severe) were established.
                           •    Vitamin D Levels: Serum vitamin D concentrations were measured in ng/mL. Defini-
                                tions for vitamin D deficiency (<20 ng/mL), insufficiency (20–30 ng/mL), and sufficiency
                                (>30 ng/mL) were standardized according to the Endocrine Society guidelines.

                           2.3. Secondary Outcomes
                           •    Quality of Life: Assessed using instruments such as the Short Form Health Survey
                                (SF-36) and the EuroQol-5D (EQ-5D).
                           •    Functional Ability: Measured using the Health Assessment Questionnaire (HAQ) and
                                the Oswestry Disability Index (ODI).
                           •    Biochemical Markers: Levels of parathyroid hormone (PTH), calcium, and phosphate
                                were recorded to provide context on the metabolic impact of vitamin D deficiency.
                           •    Sun Exposure and Dietary Intake: Evaluated using validated questionnaires and
                                dietary intake records to assess other sources of vitamin D.
                           •    Demographic and Baseline Characteristics: Data on age, gender, BMI, baseline pain
                                levels, and comorbid conditions were collected to adjust for confounding variables.

                           2.4. Quality Assessment
                                The quality of the included studies was evaluated using the NIH Quality Assessment
                           Tool for Observational Cohort and Cross-Sectional Studies. This tool consists of 14 criteria,
                           with each item rated as “cannot determine”, “not applicable”, or “not reported”. Based on
                           the overall scoring, studies were classified as “good” (11–14 points), “fair” (5–10 points),
                           or “poor” (0–4 points). For case series, the NIH Quality Assessment Tool for Case Series
                           Studies was applied.

                           2.5. Data Analysis
                                The data analysis involved grouping studies according to the presence or absence
                           of a control group, the use of sun exposure questionnaires, and the assessment of pain
                           levels in relation to vitamin D status. A qualitative analysis was conducted to explore
                           the relationships between vitamin D levels and chronic musculoskeletal pain, as well as
                           between vitamin D levels and pain intensity.

                           3. Results
                           3.1. Study Selection
                                A total of 30 observational studies investigating the relationship between vitamin D
                           levels and chronic musculoskeletal pain in adults were reviewed following the PRISMA
                           guideline. These studies were obtained by searching PubMed, Cochrane, and PEDro
                           databases, covering the period from 1990 to 2022. The selected studies met the quality
                           standards of the NHLBI guidelines.

                           3.2. Analysis and Synthesis of Results
                                The review focused on qualitatively examining the association between vitamin D
                           levels and chronic musculoskeletal pain, differences between men and women, and the
                           inverse relationship between vitamin D levels and pain intensity. It differentiated studies
                           with control groups from those without, highlighting that those with control groups provide
                           more reliable information. The review also considered the timing of blood sample collection
                           due to seasonal variations in UVA radiation affecting vitamin D levels, reflecting this in the
                           methodological quality of the studies, as shown in Table 1 [18].

                                                In Table 1, the number of selected studies that investigated the relationship between
                                           vitamin D and chronic musculoskeletal pain with a control group is gathered, amounting
                                           to 12 studies. The total number of patients analyzed was 18,136, with at least 7468 men and
                                           at least 10,567 women; the gender distribution was not defined in the study by Block, S.
                                           R. [19] (he does not provide the data in the study). Out of these studies, De Giorgi et al. [11]
                                           found a relationship between chronic pain and low vitamin D levels (below 30 ng/mL)
                                           with a total of 18,035 participants, while one study found no relationship with a total of
                                           101 participants.
                                                By country, there are six studies in Turkey, three in Egypt, two each in Iran and Brazil,
                                           and one each in Portugal, Chile, Spain, Scotland, and Israel. In one study, Atherton et al. [22]
                                           analyzed comparative data between women and men, all born in the same year, finding a
                                           positive association between low vitamin D levels and chronic pain in women but not in
                                           men. This contrasts with the study by McBeth, J. et al., which found a positive association
                                           between low vitamin D levels and chronic pain in men of different ages. Both studies used

422	                                       Erkal, et al. [21] found that there was low sun exposure in the mixed group of participants

424	                                       and that there was low sun exposure. However, the absence of a control group made it
425	                                       impossible to compare whether there was actually lower sun exposure in the group tested
426	                                       compared to a control group without chronic pain.
427	                                            In the second study, by Rezende Pena, C et al. 2010 [35], which included a sun exposure
428	                                       questionnaire and a control group, it was observed that the time of sun exposure was less in
429	                                       the patient group than in the control group, with no difference in the exposed body surface
430	                                       area. However, even with the difference in exposure, it was concluded that there was no
431	                                       difference in vitamin D levels between the two groups. It should be noted that there was a
432	                                       higher use of sunscreen in the control group, which may have affected vitamin D levels.

437	                                          In the third study, which also included a control group and a sun exposure ques-
438	                                     tionnaire, a calculation of the ultraviolet light index was conducted. The ultraviolet light
439	                                     index measures the exposure ratio in relation to the ability of the clothing worn to prevent
440	                                     exposure to solar radiation. The values obtained gave a non-significant statistical difference
441	                                     (p = 0.2) (the degree of exposure was between 0.63 and 0.03 in patients and between 0.62
442	                                     and 0.06 in the control group). This study concluded that there was no difference in vitamin
443	                                     D levels between the patient group and the control group.
444	                                          The fourth study that conducted a sun exposure questionnaire was conducted by
445	                                     Beserra, S.R. et al., 2020 [44]. The results regarding sun exposure showed that both the
446	                                     patient group and the control group had exposure of more than 30 min per day, or at least
447	                                     3–4 h per week, reaching the minimum exposure in Brazil, a country with a high level
448	                                     of sunshine throughout the year. This study concluded that they found no difference in
449	                                     vitamin D levels between the two groups.
450	                                          Once again, we observed a significant difference between the studies that had a control
451	                                     group and those without, in terms of the result and a possible association between low
452	                                     vitamin D levels and chronic musculoskeletal pain. We observe that in the studies where
453	                                     there was a control group, there is heterogeneity between one study that does observe a
454	                                     difference in sun exposure between groups and two that do not observe such a difference.

565	                                     Vitamin D and Pain Levels
566	                                          Another research question was to check for a possible association between vitamin D
567	                                     levels and pain intensity. Across the studies reviewed, the total number of patients with
568	                                     pain was 9431, while the number in the control group was 733. Of the total number of
569	                                     patients, at least 4526 were women and at least 4099 were men (one study does not specify).
570	                                     Regarding pain scales, nine studies used the VAS, nine studies used the FIQ, and among
571	                                     these nine studies, seven used both scales for pain measurement. Additionally, one study
572	                                     used the Wong-Baker Faces Pain Scale, one used the WPI, one employed PEG sensitivity
573	                                     algometry, one used manikins, and one did not specify the pain scale used.
574	                                          Out of the studies reviewed, 15 reported an association between lower vitamin D
575	                                     levels and increased pain scale scores. None of these studies specified a non-significant
576	                                     association. One study found no association between vitamin D levels and pain intensity
577	                                     on any scale.
578	                                          Among the studies that reported an association between lower vitamin D levels and
579	                                     pain, two studies observed a higher incidence of this relationship in women compared to
580	                                     men, while the others did not specify gender-based differences.
581	 Nutrients 2024, 16, 4061                                                                                             9 of 12
582	
583	
584	
585	                           4. Discussion
586	                                 This systematic review addresses the relationship between serum vitamin D levels and
587	                           CMP in adults. The evidence for a direct relationship between low vitamin D levels and the
588	                           presence of CMP remains inconclusive. However, most studies that assessed pain intensity
589	                           found an inverse relationship between vitamin D levels and pain intensity, suggesting that
590	                           while vitamin D deficiency may not directly cause CMP, it could influence its severity.
591	                                 In the results and discussion section, we noted the importance of potential confounding
592	                           factors like sun exposure and activity rate. Sun exposure is a critical determinant of vitamin
593	                           D synthesis, as ultraviolet B (UVB) radiation on the skin produces vitamin D. Variations in
594	                           geographic location, season, clothing habits, and time spent outdoors could significantly
595	                           influence serum vitamin D levels. For instance, individuals in higher latitudes or those
596	                           with cultural practices that limit skin exposure to sunlight are more likely to have vitamin
597	                           D deficiency. These differences may confound the observed association between vitamin D
598	                           levels and CMP.
599	                                 Physical activity rate is another significant confounder. Active individuals often ex-
600	                           perience improved overall health, which could influence both vitamin D status (due to
601	                           increased sun exposure) and pain intensity (due to better musculoskeletal health). Im-
602	                           portantly, physical activity itself has demonstrated analgesic effects in CMP conditions,
603	                           further complicating the isolation of vitamin D’s role in this context [48]. Studies that do not
604	                           account for these factors risk overestimating or underestimating the relationship between
605	                           vitamin D and pain outcomes [49].
606	                                 Future research should include detailed and standardized assessments of sun exposure,
607	                           accounting for factors such as seasonal variations, sunscreen use, and clothing. Additionally,
608	                           quantifying physical activity using reliable metrics will provide a clearer understanding of
609	                           its role as a confounder.
610	                                 One of the main strengths of this review is its systematic approach, which included a
611	                           wide range of observational studies, providing a comprehensive view of the topic. Quality
612	                           assessment tools further strengthen the reliability of the results.
613	                                 However, methodological variability among the included studies limits direct com-
614	                           parisons and the synthesis of findings. Many studies lacked control groups, which
615	                           weakens the ability to establish causal relationships. Additionally, the absence of specific
616	                           data on sun exposure and activity levels further complicates result interpretation. These
617	                           limitations highlight gaps in the current literature that must be addressed to draw more
618	                           robust conclusions.
619	                                 The results of this review are consistent with some previous reviews that found mixed
620	                           evidence on the relationship between vitamin D levels and chronic pain. For example,
621	                           previous reviews have found both evidence of a positive relationship and studies reporting
622	                           no significant association. The review by Martins et al. [50] and Ali et al. [51] also concluded
623	                           that the evidence is inconclusive, while the review by Ellis et al. [52] suggests a possible
624	                           positive relationship between vitamin D deficiency and pain in fibromyalgia patients.
625	
626	                           4.1. Clinical Relevance and Future Perspectives
627	                                The inverse relationship between vitamin D levels and pain intensity found in most
628	                           studies suggests that correcting vitamin D deficiency could be a useful intervention to
629	                           reduce pain intensity in patients with CMP [53–56]. This is particularly relevant given the
630	                           high prevalence of vitamin D deficiency, especially among older adults.
631	                                For clinicians, assessing and correcting vitamin D levels in patients with CMP could
632	                           provide a simple, safe, and cost-effective strategy to improve outcomes. However, it is
633	                           crucial to consider confounding factors like sun exposure and physical activity when
634	                           interpreting vitamin D levels. This underscores the need for a comprehensive approach to
635	                           evaluate the potential benefits of vitamin D supplementation.
636	                                Future studies should prioritize longitudinal designs with control groups and stan-
637	                           dardized methods for measuring both serum vitamin D and pain intensity. Detailed
638	                           assessments of sun exposure and physical activity are crucial for reducing confounding
639	 Nutrients 2024, 16, 4061                                                                                                              10 of 12
640	
641	
642	
643	                                   factors and clarifying the relationship between vitamin D and CMP. Long-term studies
644	                                   assessing the impact of vitamin D supplementation on pain outcomes will provide essential
645	                                   insights to inform clinical practice.
646	
647	                                   4.2. Limitations
648	                                        This review has notable limitations, including potential publication bias, as studies
649	                                   with positive results are more likely to be published. Additionally, only studies published
650	                                   in English were included, potentially excluding relevant findings in other languages. The
651	                                   heterogeneity of study designs and methods precluded a detailed quantitative analysis,
652	                                   limiting the precision of our conclusions.
653	
654	                                   5. Conclusions
655	                                        In conclusion, while the relationship between low vitamin D levels and CMP is not
656	                                   fully established, the evidence suggests that vitamin D may influence pain intensity. This
657	                                   review highlights the need for future research to address key confounding factors, such
658	                                   as sun exposure and activity rate, to enhance our understanding of this relationship.
659	                                   Considering vitamin D as part of CMP management strategies could provide significant
660	                                   benefits, particularly for populations at risk of deficiency.

In Table 3 we present the four studies that did take into account the sun exposure time
                                       of the participants. The first of the studies that did include the sun exposure questionnaire,
                                       Erkal, et al. [21] found that there was low sun exposure in the mixed group of participants
                                       analyzed. They concluded that there were low vitamin D levels in people with chronic pain
                                       and that there was low sun exposure. However, the absence of a control group made it
                                       impossible to compare whether there was actually lower sun exposure in the group tested
                                       compared to a control group without chronic pain.
                                            In the second study, by Rezende Pena, C et al. 2010 [35], which included a sun exposure
                                       questionnaire and a control group, it was observed that the time of sun exposure was less in
                                       the patient group than in the control group, with no difference in the exposed body surface
                                       area. However, even with the difference in exposure, it was concluded that there was no
                                       difference in vitamin D levels between the two groups. It should be noted that there was a
                                       higher use of sunscreen in the control group, which may have affected vitamin D levels.
 Nutrients 2024, 16, 4061                                                                                                      7 of 12



                                          In the third study, which also included a control group and a sun exposure ques-
                                     tionnaire, a calculation of the ultraviolet light index was conducted. The ultraviolet light
                                     index measures the exposure ratio in relation to the ability of the clothing worn to prevent
                                     exposure to solar radiation. The values obtained gave a non-significant statistical difference
                                     (p = 0.2) (the degree of exposure was between 0.63 and 0.03 in patients and between 0.62
                                     and 0.06 in the control group). This study concluded that there was no difference in vitamin
                                     D levels between the patient group and the control group.
                                          The fourth study that conducted a sun exposure questionnaire was conducted by
                                     Beserra, S.R. et al., 2020 [44]. The results regarding sun exposure showed that both the
                                     patient group and the control group had exposure of more than 30 min per day, or at least
                                     3–4 h per week, reaching the minimum exposure in Brazil, a country with a high level
                                     of sunshine throughout the year. This study concluded that they found no difference in
                                     vitamin D levels between the two groups.
                                          Once again, we observed a significant difference between the studies that had a control
                                     group and those without, in terms of the result and a possible association between low
                                     vitamin D levels and chronic musculoskeletal pain. We observe that in the studies where
                                     there was a control group, there is heterogeneity between one study that does observe a
                                     difference in sun exposure between groups and two that do not observe such a difference.

                                     3.3. Study Quality Assessment
                                          Study quality was assessed using the Quality Assessment Tool for Observational
                                     Cohort and Cross-Sectional Studies for cross-sectional studies and the Quality Assessment
                                     of Case-Control Studies for case-control studies. Most of the included studies met the
                                     minimum quality criteria, and several achieved a good quality assessment. However,
                                     heterogeneity in study designs and pain assessment methods limits the robustness of the
                                     conclusions, see Table 3.

                                     Vitamin D and Pain Levels
                                          Another research question was to check for a possible association between vitamin D
                                     levels and pain intensity. Across the studies reviewed, the total number of patients with
                                     pain was 9431, while the number in the control group was 733. Of the total number of
                                     patients, at least 4526 were women and at least 4099 were men (one study does not specify).
                                     Regarding pain scales, nine studies used the VAS, nine studies used the FIQ, and among
                                     these nine studies, seven used both scales for pain measurement. Additionally, one study
                                     used the Wong-Baker Faces Pain Scale, one used the WPI, one employed PEG sensitivity
                                     algometry, one used manikins, and one did not specify the pain scale used.
                                          Out of the studies reviewed, 15 reported an association between lower vitamin D
                                     levels and increased pain scale scores. None of these studies specified a non-significant
                                     association. One study found no association between vitamin D levels and pain intensity
                                     on any scale.
                                          Among the studies that reported an association between lower vitamin D levels and
                                     pain, two studies observed a higher incidence of this relationship in women compared to
                                     men, while the others did not specify gender-based differences.
 Nutrients 2024, 16, 4061                                                                                             9 of 12



                           4. Discussion
                                 This systematic review addresses the relationship between serum vitamin D levels and
                           CMP in adults. The evidence for a direct relationship between low vitamin D levels and the
                           presence of CMP remains inconclusive. However, most studies that assessed pain intensity
                           found an inverse relationship between vitamin D levels and pain intensity, suggesting that
                           while vitamin D deficiency may not directly cause CMP, it could influence its severity.
                                 In the results and discussion section, we noted the importance of potential confounding
                           factors like sun exposure and activity rate. Sun exposure is a critical determinant of vitamin
                           D synthesis, as ultraviolet B (UVB) radiation on the skin produces vitamin D. Variations in
                           geographic location, season, clothing habits, and time spent outdoors could significantly
                           influence serum vitamin D levels. For instance, individuals in higher latitudes or those
                           with cultural practices that limit skin exposure to sunlight are more likely to have vitamin
                           D deficiency. These differences may confound the observed association between vitamin D
                           levels and CMP.
                                 Physical activity rate is another significant confounder. Active individuals often ex-
                           perience improved overall health, which could influence both vitamin D status (due to
                           increased sun exposure) and pain intensity (due to better musculoskeletal health). Im-
                           portantly, physical activity itself has demonstrated analgesic effects in CMP conditions,
                           further complicating the isolation of vitamin D’s role in this context [48]. Studies that do not
                           account for these factors risk overestimating or underestimating the relationship between
                           vitamin D and pain outcomes [49].
                                 Future research should include detailed and standardized assessments of sun exposure,
                           accounting for factors such as seasonal variations, sunscreen use, and clothing. Additionally,
                           quantifying physical activity using reliable metrics will provide a clearer understanding of
                           its role as a confounder.
                                 One of the main strengths of this review is its systematic approach, which included a
                           wide range of observational studies, providing a comprehensive view of the topic. Quality
                           assessment tools further strengthen the reliability of the results.
                                 However, methodological variability among the included studies limits direct com-
                           parisons and the synthesis of findings. Many studies lacked control groups, which
                           weakens the ability to establish causal relationships. Additionally, the absence of specific
                           data on sun exposure and activity levels further complicates result interpretation. These
                           limitations highlight gaps in the current literature that must be addressed to draw more
                           robust conclusions.
                                 The results of this review are consistent with some previous reviews that found mixed
                           evidence on the relationship between vitamin D levels and chronic pain. For example,
                           previous reviews have found both evidence of a positive relationship and studies reporting
                           no significant association. The review by Martins et al. [50] and Ali et al. [51] also concluded
                           that the evidence is inconclusive, while the review by Ellis et al. [52] suggests a possible
                           positive relationship between vitamin D deficiency and pain in fibromyalgia patients.

                           4.1. Clinical Relevance and Future Perspectives
                                The inverse relationship between vitamin D levels and pain intensity found in most
                           studies suggests that correcting vitamin D deficiency could be a useful intervention to
                           reduce pain intensity in patients with CMP [53–56]. This is particularly relevant given the
                           high prevalence of vitamin D deficiency, especially among older adults.
                                For clinicians, assessing and correcting vitamin D levels in patients with CMP could
                           provide a simple, safe, and cost-effective strategy to improve outcomes. However, it is
                           crucial to consider confounding factors like sun exposure and physical activity when
                           interpreting vitamin D levels. This underscores the need for a comprehensive approach to
                           evaluate the potential benefits of vitamin D supplementation.
                                Future studies should prioritize longitudinal designs with control groups and stan-
                           dardized methods for measuring both serum vitamin D and pain intensity. Detailed
                           assessments of sun exposure and physical activity are crucial for reducing confounding
 Nutrients 2024, 16, 4061                                                                                                              10 of 12



                                   factors and clarifying the relationship between vitamin D and CMP. Long-term studies
                                   assessing the impact of vitamin D supplementation on pain outcomes will provide essential
                                   insights to inform clinical practice.

                                   4.2. Limitations
                                        This review has notable limitations, including potential publication bias, as studies
                                   with positive results are more likely to be published. Additionally, only studies published
                                   in English were included, potentially excluding relevant findings in other languages. The
                                   heterogeneity of study designs and methods precluded a detailed quantitative analysis,
                                   limiting the precision of our conclusions.

                                   5. Conclusions
                                        In conclusion, while the relationship between low vitamin D levels and CMP is not
                                   fully established, the evidence suggests that vitamin D may influence pain intensity. This
                                   review highlights the need for future research to address key confounding factors, such
                                   as sun exposure and activity rate, to enhance our understanding of this relationship.
                                   Considering vitamin D as part of CMP management strategies could provide significant
                                   benefits, particularly for populations at risk of deficiency.

14	  Objectives: The primary objective of this study was to analyze the correlation between the pain experienced at the time of

20	  a Numeric Pain Rating Scale (NPRS) from 0 to 10. Results: There was a significant but weak correlation between the pain
21	  experienced at the time of hamstring muscle injury and the hyperintense T2 weighted volume (r 5 0.287; P 5 0.025). There were no

24	  lesion at medical imaging. Pain at the time of injury alone seems not enough to give us a clinical meaningful indication of the MRI
25	  hyperintense T2 weighted volume.

Relationship Between the Pain Intensity at the Time
of the Hamstring Muscle Injury and the
Hyperintense T2 Weighted Volume of the Hamstring
Muscle Lesion Measured by MRI
Sylvain Grange, MD, PhD,*†‡ Ronan Plancher, MD,* Gustaav Reurink, MD,§{║ Pierre Croisille, MD, PhD,*†‡ and
Pascal Edouard, MD, PhD*§{║**††


  Abstract
  Objectives: The primary objective of this study was to analyze the correlation between the pain experienced at the time of
  a hamstring muscle injury and the hyperintense T2 weighted volume of the lesion measured on MRI. The secondary objectives were
  to analyze the differences in this pain with the lesion grade and the hamstring muscle head involved. Design: We performed
  a retrospective analysis of the data collected in a prospective, multicenter, noninterventional cohort study (HAMMER). Patients: A
  total of 61 patients were included in this analysis. Interventions: Patients with suspected hamstring muscle injury had an MRI
  after the injury. Main outcomes measures: They were evaluated for their pain intensity experienced at the time of injury with
  a Numeric Pain Rating Scale (NPRS) from 0 to 10. Results: There was a significant but weak correlation between the pain
  experienced at the time of hamstring muscle injury and the hyperintense T2 weighted volume (r 5 0.287; P 5 0.025). There were no
  significant differences in the pain according to the lesion grade (F(3,57) 5 0.982; P 5 0.408) nor according to the muscle involved
  (F(3,57) 5 1.013; P 5 0.394). Conclusions: Pain at the time of injury seemed to be weakly correlated with the extent of muscle
  lesion at medical imaging. Pain at the time of injury alone seems not enough to give us a clinical meaningful indication of the MRI
  hyperintense T2 weighted volume.
  Key Words: hamstring muscle injury, edema, MRI, extent lesion, pain
  (Clin J Sport Med 2024;00:1–6)
